title: Supply vs. Demand
hook: Same sequence, mirrored. Demand belongs to the bullish model, supply to the bearish one.

launchpad.outcome: Explain how demand and supply mirror each other: which candle forms each zone, and which boundary matters for invalidation.
launchpad.missionQuestion: How does the higher-timeframe direction decide whether you look for supply or demand?

takeaways: Demand is the bullish model. Its zone is the last bearish candle of Correction #2 before BOS #3.
Supply is the bearish model. Its zone is the last bullish candle of Correction #2 before BOS #3.
For demand, the lower boundary matters for invalidation. For supply, the upper boundary matters.
The higher-timeframe ICC direction tells you which one you’re looking for.
remember: DEMAND: BULLISH. SUPPLY: BEARISH. SAME SEQUENCE.

slides.headline: Same sequence. Mirrored.
slides.line: Demand belongs to the bullish model. Supply belongs to the bearish model. The steps don’t change, only the direction does.

slides.headline: Demand ≠ supply.
slides.line: The higher-timeframe ICC direction tells you which one you’re looking for.

points: Zone: the last bearish candle of Correction #2 before BOS #3.

check.prompt: The higher-timeframe ICC is bearish. Which zone are you looking for?

options.label: A demand zone
options.feedback: Demand belongs to the bullish model. A bearish higher-timeframe story means you look for supply.

slides.headline: Bullish model: a demand zone.
slides.line: On the 5M. BOS #1, Correction #1 and BOS #2 are already marked.

steps.caption: Correction #2 creates the demand zone: its last bearish candle. It’s potential for now.
BOS #3. A 5M close above the high Correction #2 pulled back from. The demand zone is active.
The retest. For demand, the lower boundary matters. A 5M close below it would invalidate the setup.

check.prompt: Which boundary of a demand zone matters for invalidation?

options.label: The upper boundary
options.feedback: The upper boundary is the near edge for demand. Invalidation concerns the opposite boundary: the lower one.

options.label: The lower boundary
options.why: Right. For demand, invalidation concerns the lower boundary.

slides.headline: Bearish model: a supply zone.
slides.line: On the 5M. BOS #1, Correction #1 and BOS #2 are already marked.

steps.caption: Correction #2. In the bearish model it bounces up. Look for its bullish candles.
The last bullish candle of Correction #2 creates the supply zone. It’s potential for now.
BOS #3. A 5M close below the low Correction #2 pulled back from. The supply zone is active.
The retest. For supply, the upper boundary matters. A 5M close above it would invalidate the setup.

slides.headline: Bearish model. Tap the supply candle.
slides.line: A new bearish chart. Correction #2 is marked, and the last candle is BOS #3.
slides.ask: Tap the candle that forms the supply zone.
slides.why: That’s the last bullish candle of Correction #2 before sellers produce BOS #3. It forms the supply zone.

after.caption: Supply zone. The upper boundary is the one that matters for invalidation.

slides.quote: Read the story first. Then you’ll know which zone you’re hunting.

slides.prompt: In your own words, how are demand and supply different, and which boundary matters for each?
slides.modelAnswer: Demand belongs to the bullish model: the zone is the last bearish candle of Correction #2 before BOS #3, and the lower boundary matters for invalidation. Supply belongs to the bearish model: the zone is the last bullish candle of Correction #2 before BOS #3, and the upper boundary matters for invalidation. The higher-timeframe ICC direction tells me which one to look for.
